name: tarsal tunnel posterior
aliases: tibial nerve entrapment at the ankle

clinicalPearls: Entrapment of the posterior tibial nerve or its terminal branches beneath the flexor retinaculum behind the medial malleolus, producing burning plantar pain and paraesthesiae.
Symptoms are typically worse with standing and walking and may radiate proximally along the medial calf (the Valleix phenomenon).
A Tinel sign behind the medial malleolus, and reproduction of symptoms with sustained eversion and dorsiflexion, support the diagnosis.
Selective involvement of the medial or lateral plantar branch, or the calcaneal branch, produces a restricted sensory pattern that aids localisation.
A space-occupying lesion such as a ganglion, varicosity, lipoma, accessory muscle or tenosynovitis is identified in a substantial proportion of cases and should be actively sought.
The condition is markedly less common than carpal tunnel syndrome, and overdiagnosis is a recognised problem when plantar symptoms have another cause.
Electrodiagnostic studies with distal tibial motor and mixed or sensory plantar conductions help confirm the diagnosis but can be technically difficult.
Hindfoot malalignment, particularly a valgus or planovalgus foot, increases traction on the nerve and predisposes to entrapment.
reference.pathophysiology: The posterior tibial nerve passes through the fibro-osseous tarsal tunnel behind the medial malleolus, bounded by the flexor retinaculum, where it divides into the medial and lateral plantar and calcaneal branches. Increased pressure within this confined space from a ganglion, tenosynovitis, varicosities, an accessory or hypertrophied muscle, post-traumatic fibrosis, or biomechanical traction in hindfoot valgus produces focal demyelination and axonal injury. Branch-specific compression within separate compartments accounts for the variable sensory patterns, and systemic conditions causing nerve vulnerability may lower the threshold for symptomatic entrapment.
additionalInvestigations: nerve conduction studies of medial and lateral plantar nerves with tibial motor studies
needle electromyography of intrinsic foot muscles
magnetic resonance imaging of the ankle to identify a space-occupying lesion
high-resolution ultrasound of the tarsal tunnel
weight-bearing foot radiographs to assess alignment and bony anomalies
screening for diabetes and other causes of polyneuropathy
redFlags: a rapidly enlarging or firm mass within the tarsal tunnel suggesting neoplasm
progressive motor weakness or intrinsic foot muscle wasting
constitutional symptoms or features of systemic inflammatory or infiltrative disease
bilateral or diffuse sensory loss pointing to a generalised neuropathy rather than local entrapment
reference.prognosis: Outcomes are best when a discrete compressive lesion is found and released, whereas idiopathic cases respond less predictably to decompression. Conservative measures including orthoses and corticosteroid injection help many patients with milder or biomechanical presentations.
pitfalls: diagnosing tarsal tunnel syndrome when a distal polyneuropathy is the true cause of plantar symptoms
failing to image the tunnel and thereby missing a treatable space-occupying lesion
over-interpreting technically difficult plantar nerve conduction studies
neglecting hindfoot malalignment that will cause recurrence after surgery
references: Dawson, Hallett and Wilbourn: Entrapment Neuropathies
Preston and Shapiro: Electromyography and Neuromuscular Disorders
